t.2.3.1: With its root above and its branches below, this is the eternal aśvattha tree; that alone is the bright, that is brahman, that alone is called the immortal. In it all the worlds rest, and no one ever goes beyond it. This, truly, is that.
t.2.3.3: From fear of it Agni burns, from fear of it Sūrya shines; from fear of it Indra and Vāyu, and Mṛtyu as the fifth, run about their tasks.
t.2.3.2: This whole world, whatever there is, having come forth, moves in the life-breath. Those who know this, the great terror, the upraised thunderbolt, become immortal.
t.2.3.5: As in a mirror, so is it seen in the self; as in a dream, so in the world of the fathers; as it appears all about in the waters, so in the world of the Gandharvas; as in shade and sunlight, so in the world of Brahman.
t.2.3.4: If one is able to know it here, before the body falls away, one is freed; otherwise, one becomes fit for embodiment again in the created worlds.
t.2.3.6: Knowing the separateness of the senses, which arise separately, and their rising and setting, the wise one does not grieve.
t.2.3.7: Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect, the highest; above the intellect is the great self, and higher than the great one is the unmanifest, the highest.
t.2.3.8: Beyond the Unmanifest, however, is the Puruṣa, all-pervading and without any distinguishing mark. Knowing him, a living being is set free and attains immortality.
t.2.3.9: His form does not stand within the range of sight; no one sees him with the eye. He is framed by the heart, by insight, by the mind; those who know this become immortal.
t.2.3.10: When the five organs of knowledge come to rest together with the mind, and the intellect does not stir, that, they say, is the highest state.
t.2.3.11: This firm holding of the senses they consider to be yoga. Then one becomes undistracted, for yoga is both the arising and the passing away.
t.2.3.12: Not by speech, not by mind, not by the eye can it be attained. How can it be apprehended otherwise than by one who says, "It is"?
t.2.3.13: He is to be apprehended simply as 'He is,' and also as the true being of both. For one who has apprehended him as 'He is,' his true being becomes clear.
t.2.3.14: When all the desires that dwell in his heart are cast off, then the mortal becomes immortal; here itself he attains Brahman.
t.2.3.15: When all the knots of the heart are cut asunder here, then the mortal becomes immortal. This, indeed, is the whole of the teaching.
t.2.3.17: The Person, the size of a thumb, the inner self, ever dwells in the heart of beings. One should draw him out from one's own body with steadfastness, as one draws the reed from the muñja grass. One should know him as the bright, the immortal; one should know him as the bright, the immortal.
t.2.3.16: A hundred and one are the channels of the heart; of these, one passes out toward the crown of the head. Going upward by that one, a man attains immortality; by the others, at the time of departure, he goes off in every direction.
t.2.3.18: Then, O Naciketas, having obtained this knowledge proclaimed by Death, together with the entire method of yoga, he attained Brahman and became free from passion and free from death; so too will any other who thus knows the inner Self.
